title: GOD TOLD EZEKIEL TO SHAVE HIS HEAD—THEN BURN HIS HAIR. THE REASON SHOULD MAKE EVERY CHRISTIAN TREMBLE.
paragraphs: GOD TOLD EZEKIEL TO SHAVE HIS HEAD—THEN BURN HIS HAIR. THE REASON SHOULD MAKE EVERY CHRISTIAN TREMBLE.
Three portions of hair. Three terrifying judgments. A handful preserved. And a warning written in Ezekiel 5 that still confronts every heart tempted to mistake God's patience for His approval.

Imagine waking up tomorrow and discovering that God has commanded a prophet to stand before your city, shave his head, cut off his beard, weigh every strand of hair, and then burn one portion, strike another with a sword, and scatter the rest into the wind.
You would probably think the man had lost his mind.
Until you realized...
He wasn't performing a strange religious ritual. He was showing an entire nation what was about to happen to them.
And the most frightening part?
The people watching him were not strangers to God.
They were the people who had received His covenant, His commandments, His promises, and His warnings.
They knew what worship looked like.
They knew the language of holiness.
They had the temple, the priesthood, the sacrifices, and the history of God's deliverance.
But knowing the things of God had not kept their hearts faithful to God.
And perhaps that is where this ancient prophecy begins to become painfully personal.
Because it is possible to know the words of worship while quietly surrendering your heart to something else.
It is possible to appear spiritually alive while slowly becoming comfortable with what God has called you to abandon.
It is possible to stand among God's people and still desperately need to repent.
Before we go any further, remember this:
Ezekiel's shaved head was not a lesson about hairstyles. It was a warning about judgment, covenant unfaithfulness, and the terrifying consequences of refusing to listen to God.
But hidden within that devastating picture was something else.
A few strands of hair.
A small portion that would be preserved.
And a truth about God's mercy that becomes even more astonishing when we follow the story of Scripture all the way to Jesus Christ.
Because the God who warns sinners of judgment is also the God who calls them to turn and live.
And the Gospel reveals just how far His mercy was willing to go.
Ezekiel was not standing in Jerusalem when God gave him this command.
He was among the Judean exiles in Babylon, living in a foreign land after being carried away from home.
Jerusalem still stood, but its destruction was approaching.
Many people continued to believe that their sacred city could never fall completely. Surely the temple meant they were safe. Surely their identity as God's covenant people guaranteed protection.
Yet the prophets had repeatedly warned that possessing the signs of the covenant was no substitute for faithfulness to the Lord.
And now Ezekiel was about to become a living warning.
God commanded him:
"And thou, son of man, take thee a sharp knife, take thee a barber's rasor, and cause it to pass upon thine head and upon thy beard: then take thee balances to weigh, and divide the hair."
— Ezekiel 5:1, King James Version
Read that again.
God did not merely tell Ezekiel to cut his hair.
He told him to weigh it.
To divide it carefully.
To make the destruction of Jerusalem visible through something as ordinary, intimate, and personal as the hair on a man's head.
In the Hebrew text, the command to shave uses the verb וְהַעֲבַרְתָּ (wehaʿavarta), from a root meaning to cause something to pass over or across.
Here it describes passing the cutting instrument over his head and beard.
The instrument is described using the Hebrew חֶרֶב (ḥerev), meaning a sword, followed by language identifying it as a barber's razor.
The imagery is deliberately unsettling.
An instrument associated with cutting and violence becomes the means by which the prophet removes his hair.
Then comes the command to use מֹאזְנֵי מִשְׁקָל (moʾzne mishqal)—weighing balances or scales.
Nothing about the symbolism is casual.
The hair must be divided by weight.
The coming judgment is not portrayed as an uncontrolled accident, an unfortunate coincidence, or evidence that Babylon's gods are stronger than Israel's God.
Ezekiel is announcing that Jerusalem's destruction will take place under the sovereign judgment of the Lord.
And then the command becomes even more disturbing.
God tells Ezekiel to divide the hair into three portions.
One portion must be burned.
Another must be struck with a sword.
The final portion must be scattered into the wind.
And even the scattered hair will not be beyond the reach of judgment.
What could possibly justify such a terrifying message?
The answer comes when God explains the prophecy Himself.
"This is Jerusalem: I have set it in the midst of the nations and countries that are round about her."
— Ezekiel 5:5, KJV
The hair represents Jerusalem and its people.
The city had been placed among the nations as a people called to live under God's covenant and bear witness to His holiness.
But instead of reflecting His character, Jerusalem had rebelled against His judgments and statutes.
Ezekiel 5:6–7 describes a people who had turned from God's commands.
Their privilege had not produced obedience.
Their knowledge had not produced humility.
Their religious identity had not produced covenant faithfulness.
And now the consequences were coming.
This is where the prophecy stops feeling like a distant historical curiosity.
Because we can become dangerously skilled at using spiritual language to conceal spiritual compromise.
We can say, "God knows my heart," while refusing to let His Word examine it.
We can ask for blessings while resisting correction.
We can sing about surrender while secretly protecting the one thing we refuse to surrender.
And we can mistake the fact that God has not yet confronted us with visible consequences for evidence that He approves of everything we are doing.
But God's patience is not permission to continue in sin.
Romans 2:4 teaches that God's kindness, forbearance, and patience are meant to lead us toward repentance.
Not complacency.
Not excuses.
Repentance.
And that brings us back to the three portions of Ezekiel's hair.
The first third was to be burned in the midst of the city when the days of the symbolic siege were completed.
God later explains:
"A third part of thee shall die with the pestilence, and with famine shall they be consumed in the midst of thee..."
— Ezekiel 5:12, KJV
The burning hair represented the people who would perish through famine and pestilence during the siege.
Imagine Jerusalem's streets.
Families running out of food.
Parents unable to protect their children from hunger.
The security they had taken for granted disappearing.
The city they believed could never fall becoming a place of unbearable suffering.
This was not an invitation to enjoy imagining the pain of others.
It was a dreadful warning of the consequences of covenant rebellion and the catastrophe of siege warfare.
God was telling His people what was coming before it came.
And that matters.
Because divine warnings are not given merely to satisfy curiosity about the future.
They confront the present.
They expose the direction of a life, a people, or a nation.
They summon hearers to take God's Word seriously.
The second third of the hair was to be struck with the sword around the city.
Ezekiel 5:12 explains that another third would fall by the sword.
Babylon's military assault would bring death.
The defenses of Jerusalem would not save everyone.
Its walls would not guarantee deliverance.
And the sword would reach those who had placed their confidence in what could not ultimately protect them.
There is something deeply sobering here.
The things people trust most can become the very things that reveal how fragile their security really is.
Money can disappear.
Reputation can collapse.
Influence can fade.
Health can change.
Human approval can vanish overnight.
None of these things can reconcile a sinner to God.
And although Ezekiel's specific judgment concerns ancient Jerusalem, the spiritual danger of misplaced confidence remains real.
We may not bow before carved idols, but the human heart still manufactures false saviors.
Some people worship success.
Some worship control.
Some worship the approval of others.
Some cling to secret sins because the thought of surrender feels more frightening than the thought of judgment.
And some have spent years maintaining a Christian appearance while quietly losing their hunger for Christ.
Perhaps nobody knows how exhausted you have become from pretending.
Perhaps you have learned how to smile in church while carrying guilt you cannot explain.
Perhaps you still believe in Jesus, but you know there are areas of your life where you have stopped listening to Him.
If that is you, do not mistake conviction for a declaration that you are beyond hope.
The purpose of bringing hidden things into the light is not to convince you that Christ cannot receive you.
It is to stop you from running away from the One who can forgive, cleanse, and restore you.
Now look at the third portion of Ezekiel's hair.
God commanded the prophet to scatter it into the wind.
Ezekiel 5:12 explains that the surviving third would be scattered, and the sword would pursue them.
The people who escaped the immediate destruction would face dispersion and continuing danger.
Their homeland would be lost.
Their familiar lives would be shattered.
Their world would never be the same.
Burned.
Struck.
Scattered.
Three portions of hair.
Three dimensions of judgment.
And an entire city confronted with the consequences of its rebellion.
But then something extraordinary happens in the prophecy.
God tells Ezekiel:
"Thou shalt also take thereof a few in number, and bind them in thy skirts."
— Ezekiel 5:3, KJV
A few strands.
Not a large bundle.
Not enough to make the scene look hopeful by human standards.
Just a few.
And Ezekiel must gather them and bind them in the folds of his garment.
The Hebrew uses מְעַט בְּמִסְפָּר (meʿat bemispar), meaning a small number or few in number.
The command to bind them comes from the Hebrew root צָרַר (tsarar), which can mean to bind, wrap, or bundle together.
The prophet must keep these few hairs close in his garment.
After all the burning, cutting, and scattering, a small portion is set apart.
It is a striking picture.
Yet we must read it carefully.
Ezekiel 5:4 immediately adds that some of those hairs are also to be taken and thrown into the fire.
The preserved handful is not a simplistic promise that every person initially spared will escape all further judgment.
The passage emphasizes how severe and far-reaching Jerusalem's judgment will be.

Nevertheless, the imagery of a small preserved portion fits within the larger biblical theme of God's preservation of a remnant, a theme that becomes clearer elsewhere in Ezekiel and throughout the prophets.
God's judgment upon Jerusalem did not mean His covenant purposes had failed.
Later, in Ezekiel 11:16–20, the Lord promises to be a sanctuary to His scattered people, to gather them, and to give them a new heart and a new spirit.
And in Ezekiel 36:26–27, He declares:
"A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you..."
— Ezekiel 36:26, KJV
Do you see the movement?
Ezekiel 5 shows the devastating consequences of a rebellious heart.
Ezekiel 36 announces God's promise to give His people a new heart.
The problem was deeper than Jerusalem's walls.
Deeper than its political leaders.
Deeper than its military defenses.
The people needed inward renewal.
They needed more than a repaired city.
They needed hearts transformed by God.
And this is where the story begins to point us toward the astonishing beauty of Jesus Christ.
Not because Ezekiel's three portions of hair are a secret code predicting three events in Jesus' life.
Scripture does not teach that.
And we do not need to force such symbolism onto the text to discover Christ-centered hope.
The connection is greater, deeper, and rooted in the unfolding message of the Bible.
The holy God who judged Jerusalem's rebellion is the same holy God who promises a new covenant, forgiveness, and transformed hearts.
The judgment announced by Ezekiel reveals the seriousness of sin.
The promises that follow reveal the mercy and faithfulness of God.
And the New Testament announces that Jesus Christ is the mediator of the new covenant.
Hebrews 8:6–12 connects that new covenant with God's promise to forgive sins and remember them no more.
At the cross, Jesus did not announce that sin was harmless.
He bore the judgment sinners deserved so that those who trust in Him might be forgiven and reconciled to God.
The apostle Paul writes:
— 2 Corinthians 5:21, KJV
The Greek text includes the phrase ἁμαρτίαν ἐποίησεν (hamartian epoiēsen)—literally, "He made [him] sin."
This does not mean Jesus became morally sinful.
Paul explicitly says that Christ knew no sin.
Rather, the language speaks of the sinless Christ being appointed to bear sin on our behalf, so that through union with Him believers receive righteousness before God.
Consider what that means.
The One who never rebelled against His Father willingly entered the suffering of the cross.
The One who deserved no condemnation endured death for sinners.
The One who had no guilt of His own became the Savior of the guilty.
And the One who was laid in a tomb rose again.
This is not merely an inspiring ending to a tragic story.
It is the heart of the Gospel.
Jesus Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again on the third day, as proclaimed in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
He did not come merely to make religious people feel better about themselves.
He came to save sinners.
To call them to repentance.
To forgive.
To reconcile.
To give new life.
To make people new.
And this is why our message is not simply that scandal can be forgotten.
It is that grace can transform the person whose life has been marked by scandal.
Not by pretending the past never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by removing every earthly consequence.
But by forgiving sin, changing hearts, restoring fellowship with God, and giving believers a new identity in Christ.
There is a difference between hiding your past and being redeemed from it.
Hiding says, "I hope nobody ever discovers who I was."
Grace says, "Jesus knows the truth about me, and He is still able to save."
Hiding keeps you imprisoned by the fear of exposure.
Grace invites you to confess, repent, and walk in the light.
Hiding teaches you to perform holiness.
Grace teaches you to depend on Christ for genuine transformation.
And perhaps the most painful thing about Ezekiel's prophecy is realizing how long people can resist God's voice before they finally understand what they have been refusing to hear.
But listen carefully.
You are reading this today.
You are not being asked to reconstruct Jerusalem's siege.
You are being invited to consider the condition of your own heart in the light of Scripture.
Are you walking with Jesus, or have you become comfortable merely looking like someone who does?
Is there a sin you keep excusing because you have not yet experienced its consequences?
Is there someone you need to forgive?
Is there dishonesty you need to confess?
Is there a relationship, habit, or hidden compromise that has been slowly drawing your heart away from Christ?
These are not questions meant to make you despair.
They are questions worth bringing honestly before the Lord.
Because the Gospel does not end with exposure.
It opens the door to repentance, forgiveness, and restoration.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Notice the promise.
Faithful.
Just.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Not because confession earns salvation.
Not because tears can purchase mercy.
Not because we can undo the damage of yesterday through our own efforts.
But because forgiveness rests upon the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And when someone truly comes to Him in repentance and faith, that person is not beyond His power to redeem.
The enemy of your soul would love for you to believe that the worst thing you have done must be the final word over your life.
But Jesus Christ is greater than your worst chapter.
Your sin is serious.
Your choices matter.
Your repentance must be genuine.
Yet your failures do not have greater saving power than the blood of Christ.
There is mercy for the repentant sinner.
There is hope for the believer who has wandered.
There is grace for the person who is finally tired of hiding.
And there is a Savior who does not need you to manufacture a flawless past before you come to Him.
He calls you to come honestly.
To turn from sin.
To trust Him.
To follow Him.
Maybe you have been carrying a secret for years.
Maybe your family knows only the version of you that you allow them to see.
Maybe you have prayed the same prayer a hundred times because you keep returning to the same struggle.
Maybe you are ashamed that your spiritual life has become so cold.
Or maybe you have been hurt by someone who used the name of God while behaving nothing like Christ.
Whatever your story, do not confuse the failures of human beings with the character of Jesus.
Look to Him.
He is holy.
He is merciful.
He is truthful.
He does not excuse sin, and He does not despise the brokenhearted who turn to Him.
Ezekiel himself later records these words from the Lord:
"For I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth, saith the Lord GOD: wherefore turn yourselves, and live ye."
— Ezekiel 18:32, KJV
In Hebrew, the call to turn is expressed through שׁוּבוּ (shuvu), from the verb שׁוּב (shuv), meaning to turn or return.
It is a summons to abandon the path of rebellion and return to God.
Not simply to feel bad.
Not merely to fear consequences.
But to turn.
And live.
That is what makes the message of Ezekiel so piercing.
The God who warned Jerusalem about coming destruction also revealed His desire for the wicked to turn from their ways.
Ezekiel 33:11 repeats this truth with remarkable urgency.
God's judgment is real.
His holiness is not negotiable.
But His call to repentance is also real.
And through Jesus Christ, the invitation to receive forgiveness is proclaimed to the world.
Perhaps this is the moment to stop saying, "One day I will get serious about my faith."
Perhaps it is time to stop postponing the apology.
To stop defending the secret sin.
To stop confusing church attendance with spiritual surrender.
To stop running from the God who has been calling you to return.
You do not have to know how to repair every broken piece of your life before taking the next faithful step.
You can begin by telling God the truth.
"Lord, I have sinned."
"Lord, I have been pretending."
"Lord, I need Your mercy."
"Lord Jesus, I believe You died and rose again. Forgive me, change my heart, and teach me to follow You."
Not a magic formula.
Not a performance.
An honest response of repentance and faith to the Savior revealed in Scripture.
And if you have already trusted in Christ, remember that spiritual growth is not the absence of every struggle.
It is a life of continuing dependence on Him, repentance when we sin, obedience to His Word, and growth through the work of the Holy Spirit.
Do not turn conviction into hopelessness.
Let it lead you back to Christ.
If this message has uncovered something you have been avoiding, I want to invite you into an honest moment.
You do not need to reveal private details publicly. God knows what you are carrying.
There are moments when a small confession of need can become the beginning of a much deeper conversation, a prayer, or a step toward seeking wise pastoral care and support.
And please, do not let this message end with you.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list may be a person who has quietly stopped praying.
Someone who is ashamed to return to church.
Someone who believes that after everything they have done, God could never welcome them again.
Someone who needs to hear that judgment is real, repentance matters, and Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to publicly expose their struggles.
But to invite them to encounter the Word of God.

If this kind of Scripture-centered message has helped you, consider following Gospel Warrior and inviting others to follow as well—believers who want to grow, seekers who are asking honest questions, and people who may be struggling to find their way back to Christ.

We want it to be a place where Scripture is opened carefully, where difficult passages are explained faithfully, where the Gospel is proclaimed clearly, and where people are continually directed toward Jesus Christ.
It does not purchase forgiveness, salvation, blessings, or a higher standing before the Lord.
Those gifts cannot be bought.
Salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by works or financial contributions, as Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not come through pressure or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.

So if you already set aside part of your personal giving for Christian ministry, you may prayerfully consider including Gospel Warrior among the ministries you support, while remaining faithful to the responsibilities and commitments God has placed before you.
It should not replace your responsibility to support your local church or those who depend on you.
Those free resources remain an important part of our mission.
These products can serve as personal reminders of faith, gifts for loved ones, or practical tools for study and reflection.
It is the opportunity to help more people encounter the truth of Scripture.
To help a discouraged believer find biblical encouragement.
To help someone understand a passage they once found confusing.
To help a searching soul hear about the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
And to help us keep sharing the message that grace is not permission to remain unchanged, but the power of God at work in those who belong to Christ.
Our goal is not to build a following around a personality.
It is to point people toward the Savior.
Because one day the posts will be forgotten.
The algorithms will change.
The platforms may disappear.
The products will wear out.
But the Word of our God will stand forever.
And the souls of people matter far more than any number on a screen.
Now, before you leave, return with me to that strange scene in Ezekiel.
A prophet standing with a razor.
Hair falling to the ground.
Scales weighing what has been cut away.
A portion consumed by fire.
Another struck by a sword.
Another scattered to the wind.
And a few strands gathered into the folds of a garment.
The scene was a warning to Jerusalem.
A terrible announcement that covenant rebellion would not go unanswered.
But the book of Ezekiel does not end with Jerusalem's ruin.
It moves toward God's promises of restoration, cleansing, a new heart, and His presence among His people.
And when we read those promises in the light of the New Testament, we are led to Jesus Christ, the One through whom forgiveness and new-covenant life are given.
That is the hope I want you to carry away.
Not that your life will never suffer consequences.
Not that repentance erases every wound overnight.
Not that following Jesus guarantees an easy future.
But that through His death and resurrection, forgiveness is real, reconciliation with God is possible, and a transformed life can begin.
So do not walk away from this passage merely remembering that Ezekiel shaved his head.
Remember why God told him to do it.
Remember that holiness matters.
Remember that warnings are worth hearing.
Remember that repentance must never be treated lightly.
And above all, remember the Savior who calls sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
The most dangerous thing is not discovering how far you have wandered—it is hearing the voice calling you home and deciding not to return.
